19189002.extract:
# 2010 NFC Championship Game

The 2010 NFC Championship Game was a National Football League playoff game played on January 24, 2010, at the Louisiana Superdome in New Orleans, Louisiana, between the New Orleans Saints and the Minnesota Vikings to determine the NFC representative in Super Bowl XLIV. New Orleans defeated Minnesota 31–28 in overtime on Garrett Hartley’s 40-yard field goal, sending the Saints to the first Super Bowl in franchise history. Minnesota outgained New Orleans 475–257 and led in first downs and time of possession, but committed five turnovers to the Saints’ one. The game featured several pivotal late sequences, including a Vikings penalty for 12 men in the huddle in the final minute of regulation and Brett Favre’s interception by Tracy Porter that sent the game to overtime, where the Saints won the coin toss and scored on the opening possession. The contest drew one of the largest audiences in conference championship history on Fox and is frequently discussed in the context of subsequent NFL overtime rule reforms adopted later in 2010 for the postseason and extended to the regular season in 2012. The Saints’ defensive hits on Favre in this game also became a focal point in media coverage of the NFL’s 2012 investigation into a New Orleans “bounty” program, which led to significant organizational sanctions and later appellate rulings on player discipline. 

## Background

- Teams and seeds: The Saints entered the game as the NFC’s top seed after a 13–3 regular season, while the Vikings were the No. 2 seed at 12–4. Minnesota had routed the Dallas Cowboys in the Divisional Round, while New Orleans had advanced from the other Divisional matchup to host the championship. Brad Childress coached the Vikings; Sean Payton coached the Saints, with Gregg Williams as New Orleans’ defensive coordinator. The winner advanced to Super Bowl XLIV. 

- Venue and administration: The game was played indoors at the Louisiana Superdome on an artificial surface. Kickoff was at 5:45 p.m. CST, and attendance was 71,276. The referee was Pete Morelli. New Orleans won the overtime coin toss. 

## Game summary

### First half

Minnesota opened with a 10-play, 80-yard drive capped by Adrian Peterson’s 19-yard touchdown run at 9:35 of the first quarter for a 7–0 lead. New Orleans answered on a 38-yard screen pass from Drew Brees to Pierre Thomas at 6:30 to tie 7–7. The Vikings regained the lead when Brett Favre found Sidney Rice for a 5-yard touchdown with 2:11 left in the first quarter, making it 14–7. New Orleans tied again in the second quarter on Brees’s 9-yard touchdown pass to Devery Henderson at 10:30, and the teams went to halftime even at 14–14. Late in the half, Reggie Bush muffed a punt at the New Orleans 10-yard line, but a botched Favre–Peterson exchange moments later gave the ball back to the Saints and preserved the tie. 

### Second half

New Orleans took its first lead early in the third quarter. After Courtney Roby’s 61-yard kickoff return opened the half, Pierre Thomas scored on a 9-yard run at 12:56 for a 21–14 Saints lead. Minnesota tied the game on Peterson’s 1-yard touchdown at 7:35 of the third. New Orleans went ahead 28–21 in the fourth quarter when Brees hit Reggie Bush for a 5-yard touchdown at 12:39, a drive set up by a Percy Harvin fumble at the Vikings’ 22-yard line. Peterson’s 2-yard touchdown with 4:58 remaining tied the game 28–28. With 1:59 left in regulation, Saints linebacker Jonathan Vilma intercepted Favre at the New Orleans 28, but the Saints punted. Minnesota then drove into long field-goal range before being penalized for 12 men in the huddle with just over a minute left, moving the ball back from the New Orleans 33-yard line and complicating the kick attempt. On the ensuing play, under pressure and rolling right, Favre threw late across his body toward Sidney Rice and was intercepted by Tracy Porter at the New Orleans 22 with 19 seconds left, sending the game to overtime. 

### Overtime

New Orleans won the overtime coin toss and received the kickoff. Courtney Roby returned it 40 yards to the Saints’ 39-yard line. The Saints’ possession included a defensive holding penalty that produced an automatic first down, a successful fourth-and-inches conversion by Pierre Thomas that was upheld on review, and a defensive pass interference penalty on Vikings linebacker Ben Leber that advanced the ball to the Minnesota 29. A subsequent 12-yard completion from Brees to Robert Meachem to the Vikings’ 22 was confirmed on review. After the drive stalled, Hartley connected from 40 yards 4:45 into the overtime for the 31–28 win. 

## Scoring summary

- 1st quarter
 - 9:35 MIN – Adrian Peterson 19-yard run (Ryan Longwell kick). Vikings 7–0. 
 - 6:30 NO – Pierre Thomas 38-yard pass from Drew Brees (Garrett Hartley kick). 7–7. 
 - 2:11 MIN – Sidney Rice 5-yard pass from Brett Favre (Longwell kick). Vikings 14–7. 

- 2nd quarter
 - 10:30 NO – Devery Henderson 9-yard pass from Brees (Hartley kick). 14–14. 

- 3rd quarter
 - 12:56 NO – Pierre Thomas 9-yard run (Hartley kick). Saints 21–14. 
 - 7:35 MIN – Peterson 1-yard run (Longwell kick). 21–21. 

- 4th quarter
 - 12:39 NO – Reggie Bush 5-yard pass from Brees (Hartley kick). Saints 28–21. 
 - 4:58 MIN – Peterson 2-yard run (Longwell kick). 28–28. 

- Overtime
 - 10:15 NO – Garrett Hartley 40-yard field goal. Saints 31–28 (OT). 

## Statistics

- Team totals: Minnesota outgained New Orleans 475–257, led 31–15 in first downs and 36:49–27:56 in time of possession, and converted 7 of 12 third downs; New Orleans converted 3 of 12. Minnesota committed five turnovers (two interceptions, three lost fumbles); New Orleans had one lost fumble. Red zone efficiency: Minnesota 4-of-6; New Orleans 3-of-3. Penalties: Vikings 5 for 32 yards; Saints 9 for 88 yards. 

- Individual leaders:
 - Vikings: Brett Favre 28-for-46, 310 yards, 1 TD, 2 INT; Adrian Peterson 25 rushes, 122 yards, 3 TD; Bernard Berrian 9 receptions, 102 yards; Visanthe Shiancoe 4 for 83; Sidney Rice 4 for 43 and 1 TD. 
 - Saints: Drew Brees 17-for-31, 197 yards, 3 TD, 0 INT (sacked once); Pierre Thomas 14 rushes, 61 yards, 1 TD; receiving TDs by Thomas (38 yards), Devery Henderson (9 yards), and Reggie Bush (5 yards). Courtney Roby had 5 kickoff returns for 143 yards (long 61). Garrett Hartley was 4-for-4 on PATs and 1-for-1 on field goals (40 yards). 

- Notable defensive plays: New Orleans interceptions by Tracy Porter (returned 26 yards) and Jonathan Vilma (3 yards). Key Vikings fumbles included a late second-quarter center–exchange fumble deep in Saints territory and fourth-quarter fumbles by Bernard Berrian at the Saints’ 10 and Percy Harvin at the Vikings’ 22. 

## Officiating and rules context

The game was officiated by referee Pete Morelli’s crew. The Saints’ overtime drive included multiple replay reviews—on a fourth-and-inches conversion by Pierre Thomas and on a 12-yard completion to Robert Meachem—and was extended by defensive holding and a defensive pass interference foul on Vikings linebacker Ben Leber before Hartley’s winning 40-yarder. 

At the NFL Annual Meeting in March 2010, owners voted 28–4 to adopt a modified sudden-death overtime format for the postseason beginning with the 2010 season. Under the change, a field goal on the opening possession no longer ends the game; the opponent is guaranteed a possession unless the first-drive result is a touchdown. The league subsequently extended the modified system to the regular season at the 2012 Annual Meeting by a 30–2 vote; regular-season overtime could end in a tie after one 15-minute period, while postseason overtime continued until a winner was determined. Contemporary reporting and league materials describe the procedures and rationale for the change. 

## Controversies and aftermath

- Bounty scandal context: In 2012, the NFL announced that its Security Department had found that Saints defensive personnel operated a pay-for-performance “bounty” program during the 2009–2011 seasons, including allegations of rewards for “cart-offs” and “knockouts” and an alleged bounty targeting Brett Favre before this championship game. The league imposed major sanctions on the organization and team leaders: a $500,000 fine and forfeiture of second-round draft picks in 2012 and 2013 for the club; a season-long suspension without pay for head coach Sean Payton in 2012; an indefinite suspension for former defensive coordinator Gregg Williams; an eight-game suspension for general manager Mickey Loomis; and a six-game suspension for assistant head coach Joe Vitt. The league stated that player discipline would be handled separately. 

 Former NFL Commissioner Paul Tagliabue, appointed as appeals officer, later vacated all player suspensions in December 2012 while affirming factual findings that a program existed and that certain players engaged in conduct detrimental, concluding that organizational misconduct and procedural issues warranted vacatur of player suspensions. Sanctions for coaches and executives were not part of the player appeal and remained in effect. Coverage and the full decision emphasized that while player suspensions were vacated, the existence of a pay-for-performance program and organizational responsibility stood. 

- Late-game sequences and officiating scrutiny: The Vikings’ “12 men in the huddle” penalty in the final minute of regulation moved the ball back from the New Orleans 33-yard line and preceded Favre’s interception by Tracy Porter at the Saints’ 22-yard line with 0:19 left. In overtime, a defensive pass interference penalty on Ben Leber helped move the Saints into field-goal range; team outlets described the foul as controversial at the time. 

## Broadcast and ratings

The game aired on Fox and drew one of the largest audiences for a conference championship telecast. Fast-national Nielsen estimates showed an average of 57.9 million viewers and a 30.6 household rating/45 share, peaking at approximately 65.2 million viewers and a 34.4/48 rating as the game neared overtime. According to Sports Media Watch, the telecast ranks among the most-watched and highest-rated NFL conference championship games in modern measurement and was, at the time, the most-viewed non–Super Bowl program on any network since the 1998 Seinfeld finale. Fox reported extraordinary local ratings in New Orleans (63.2/82, peaking at 67.4/86 during Hartley’s kick) and Minneapolis–St. Paul (58.7/80). 

## Outcome and significance

New Orleans won 31–28 on Hartley’s 40-yard overtime field goal after securing the overtime coin toss and driving into range on the opening possession. The victory sent the Saints to Super Bowl XLIV, the franchise’s first Super Bowl appearance. The Vikings’ statistical advantages in yardage, first downs, and possession were offset by five turnovers, including late-game giveaways in scoring territory. The game’s dramatic finish, officiating decisions under then-prevailing overtime rules, and physical play against Brett Favre figured prominently in subsequent debates about overtime equity and in the league’s 2012 discipline related to the Saints’ pay-for-performance program.

4.title: N.F.C. Championship Final: Saints 31, Vikings 28 (Overtime)
4.description: Thayer Evans and Joe Lapointe were in New Orleans providing live analysis of the National Football Conference championship game Sunday between the Vikings and the Saints.
4.content:
![Image 1: Saints kicker Garrett Hartley was surrounded by teammates after his winning field goal against the Minnesota Vikings in the N.F.C. Championship on Sunday.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/01/25/sports/25nfc04/blogSpan.jpg)Jed Jacobsohn/Getty Images Saints kicker Garrett Hartley was surrounded by teammates after his winning field goal against the Minnesota Vikings in the N.F.C. Championship on Sunday.

[![Image 2: Minnesota Vikings](https://static01.nyt.com/images/blogs_v3/fifthdown/teams/vikings75.jpg)](https://archive.nytimes.com/fifthdown.blogs.nytimes.com/tag/vikings/ "VIKINGS - The Fifth Down Blog - NYTimes.com")

[![Image 3: New Orleans Saints](https://static01.nyt.com/images/blogs_v3/fifthdown/teams/saints75.jpg)](https://archive.nytimes.com/fifthdown.blogs.nytimes.com/tag/saints/ "SAINTS - The Fifth Down Blog - NYTimes.com")

_Thayer Evans and Joe Lapointe were in New Orleans providing live analysis of the N.F.C. championship game Sunday between the Vikings and the Saints._

NEW ORLEANS — Garrett Hartley lifted the New Orleans Saints into their first Super Bowl with a 40-yard field goal in overtime for a [31-28 victory](https://www.nfl.com/gamecenter/2010012401/2009/POST20/vikings@saints#tab:watch) Sunday against the Minnesota Vikings in the National Football Conference championship.

A battered Brett Favre threw away Minnesota’s chance for its first Super Bowl trip in 33 years with an interception deep in Saints territory in the final seconds of regulation. New Orleans won the coin toss, Drew Brees guided it to the Minnesota 22 and Hartley, who had been suspended at the start of the season for using a banned stimulant, split the uprights 4 minutes 45 seconds into overtime.

“Just helping my team get to Miami,” Hartley said. “Just doing my part.”

Brees completed 17 of 31 passes for 197 yards and 3 touchdowns. Favre was 28 of 46 for 310 yards, with a touchdown and two interceptions. Minnesota’s Adrian Peterson rushed for 122 yards on 25 carries. He scored three touchdowns but fumbled twice. The Vikings lost three of their six fumbles.

The Saints (15-3) will meet Peyton Manning and the Indianapolis Colts (16-2) in the Super Bowl on Feb. 7 in Miami Gardens, Fla. It’s the first time the [top seeds in each conference](https://sportsillustrated.cnn.com/statitudes/news/2002/01/21/topseeds_superbowl/) made the Super Bowl since the 1993 season.

**Update | 10:20 p.m.**Hartley’s 40-yard kick is good. **The Saints win, 31-28**, and are headed to their first Super Bowl. The gold and black confetti is raining down in the Superdome. Get ready for another two weeks of Who Dat as the Saints are headed to Miami Gardens, Fla., to play the Indianapolis Colts in Super Bowl XLIV. — _TE_

**Update | 10:18 p.m.**Brees throws incomplete on third down. It’s up to Saints kicker Garrett Hartley. He’s staring down a 40-yard field-goal attempt. — _TE_

**Update | 10:16 p.m.**Bush is tackled for a 5-yard loss, but Brees then throws a 12-yard pass to Robert Meachem, who bobbled it coming down at the Vikings’ 22. The catch was upheld upon review. — _TE_

**Update | 10:14 p.m.**Vikings linebacker Ben Leber gets called for a 12-yard pass interference penalty on Saints’ David Thomas. It’s a questionable call; both players’ legs appeared to get caught up. Nonetheless, it’s a first down for the Saints at the Vikings’ 29-yard line. — _TE_

**Update | 10:09 p.m.**Still short. Not surprisingly, the Saints are going for it. They pick up 2 yards for a first down, but the booth is reviewing the play.

Replay confirms first down for the Saints. — _TE_

**Update | 10:06 p.m.**Henderson makes a 9-yard reception to the Vikings’ 43, but is short of a first down according to the measurement. It’s fourth-and a foot or two. The booth is reviewing the spot. — _TE_

**Update | 10:03 p.m.**An automatic first down for Saints on a 5-yard holding penalty by the Vikings. The Saints are at their own 48-yard line. — _TE_

**Update | 10:01 p.m.**It’s the Saints’ game to lose. They have ideal field position and probably need 25 yards to get into field-goal range. — _TE_

**Update | 9:59 p.m.**A big kickoff return for 40 yards by Thomas to the Saints’ 39-yard line. — _TE_

**Update | 9:57 p.m.**New Orleans wins the toss and will receive. This will be the third N.F.C. Championship game to be decided in overtime. — _TE_

**Update | 9:54 p.m.**Interception. Farve picked off by Saints cornerback Tracy Porter, who returns it to the New Orleans 48-yard line. Favre was trying to force a pass to Rice.

The Saints run out the clock in regulation, with the **score tied at 28-28**. The trip to the Super Bowl will be decided in overtime. — _TE_

**Update | 9:53 p.m.**Vikings just flagged 5 yards for having 12 players in huddle. That moves the ball back to the 38-yard line, with 19 seconds left and third-and-15. — _TE_

**Update | 9:51 p.m.**Peterson carries the ball to the Saints’ 33 with 19 seconds left. Vikings call timeout. Kicker Ryan Longwell warming up. — _TE_

**Update | 9:49 p.m.**Vikings convert a huge third-and-8 on Favre’s 10-yard pass to Berrian. Favre then completes a 20-yard pass to the Saints’ 47-yard line. Another 14-yard pass by Favre. Minnesota has ball at Saints’ 33 with 1:06 left. The Vikings are in field goal range. — _TE_

**Update | 9:44 p.m.**We’ve reached the **two-minute warning**. Score is tied at 28-28 and Minnesota has the ball at its own 21 facing second-and-10. There’s a lot of anxiety in the air. Saints fans don’t seem as confident as they once did. Who wants to go the Super Bowl? — _TE_

**Update | 9:42 p.m.**New Orleans continues to be fortunate. Brees was sacked on the Saints’ first play and fumbled, but his team recovered it. They just punted and Minnesota has it at their own 21 with 2:37 left and the game tied at 28-28. — _TE_

**Update | 9:38 p.m.**Now, it’s gut-check time for the Saints. Their offense has essentially sputtered since scoring a touchdown to open the second half. This could be the drive that takes them to their first Super Bowl. They’re starting at their own 20-yard line with less than five minutes left in the game. — _TE_

![Image 4: Adrian Peterson ran 18 yards for his third touchdown, tying the game 28-28 in the fourth quarter.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/01/25/sports/25vikingsH/blogSpan.jpg)Chris Graythen/Getty Images Adrian Peterson ran 18 yards for his third touchdown, tying the game 28-28 in the fourth quarter.

**Update | 9:33 p.m.**So here comes Minnesota. Needing a touchdown to tie, the Vikings marched to the Saints’ 19-yard line, and Peterson’s 18-yard touchdown run **tied the score at 28-28** with less than six minutes left.

The touchdown was set up by a defensive pass interference penalty. The Superdome is quiet again. — _TE_

**Update | 9:27 p.m.**New Orleans just unsuccessfully challenged whether Brees rushed for a first down on third-and-1 at its own 14-yard line. It punted and the Vikings have the ball at their own 43 with 7:57 left in the fourth quarter. — _TE_

**Update | 9:24 p.m.**Berrian just fumbled after making an 8-yard reception, and the Saints recovered at their own 5-yard line. That’s the third lost fumble for the Vikings today, and perhaps their most costly. — _TE_

**Update | 9:21 p.m.**A big-time throw by Favre for 30 yards to the Saints’ 20-yard line. He may be 40 years old, but he’s still a warrior. — _TE_

**Update | 9:19 p.m.**Peterson just broke a 27-yard run to midfield. The Vikings are going to need more of that down the stretch because Favre is still hobbling. His offensive line isn’t helping him much, either. He just took another big hit on an incompletion. — _TE_

**Update | 9:16 p.m.**The Superdome is rocking again. Minnesota takes over at its own 20-yard line with less than 13 minutes left. This is another pivotal possession for the Vikings. Can Favre rally his team again? — _TE_

![Image 5: After a review by the officials, New Orleans went ahead, 28-21, on Brees’s 5-yard touchdown pass to a twisting Reggie Bush.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/01/25/sports/25vikingsG/blogSpan.jpg)Sean Gardner/Reuters After a review by the officials, New Orleans went ahead, 28-21, on Brees’s 5-yard touchdown pass to a twisting Reggie Bush.

**Update | 9:13 p.m.**Harvin’s fumble was costly, because after a review by the officials, **New Orleans went ahead, 28-21**, on Brees’s 5-yard touchdown pass to Bush with 12:39 left in the fourth quarter. — _TE_

**Update | 9:10 p.m.**Minnesota’s fumble problems continue. Harvin just lost one at his own 22, and it was recovered by Ayodele, who returned it 11 yards to the Vikings’ 7. — _TE_

**Update | 9:07 p.m.**Favre is back on the field at the start of the fourth quarter. He is still hobbling after making a handoff. — _TE_

**Update | 8:57 p.m.**Favre hobbled off the field with assistance from trainers after throwing an interception at the New Orleans 28 and being crushed on a high hit by Saints defensive tackle Remi Ayodele and a low hit by defensive end Bobby McCray. New Orleans linebacker Jonathan Vilma made the interception and returned it 3 yards to the Saints 31. The Saints took over with 1:59 left in the third quarter.

The injury appeared to be to Favre’s left ankle. At least that’s what trainers were working on. His left ankle appeared as purple as his uniform and was getting taped. — _TE_

**Update | 8:51 p.m.**New Orleans couldn’t answer Minnesota and punted. The Vikings took over at their own 10-yard line after a 63-yard punt. Peterson nearly gave it away two plays later, but recovered his own fumble on a 15-yard run to the Minnesota 32. It was Peterson’s second fumble of the game. — _TE_

**Update | 8:46 p.m.**Leave it to Favre to come through for his team when needed. On the Vikings’ last scoring drive, he was 5 of 5 passing for 85 yards. That’s what you’d expect from a three-time N.F.L. most valuable player and a Super Bowl champion. — _TE_

![Image 6: Adrian Peterson (28) drove through Saints linebacker Marvin Mitchell (50) for a 1-yard touchdown in the third quarter.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/01/25/sports/25vikingsF/blogSpan.jpg)David J. Phillip/Associated Press Adrian Peterson (28) drove through Saints linebacker Marvin Mitchell (50) for a 1-yard touchdown in the third quarter.

**Update | 8:40 p.m.**Peterson just made up for his fumble earlier in the drive with a 1-yard touchdown run to **tie the game at 21-21** with 7:35 left in the third quarter. The nine-play, 80-yard drive was just the answer that Minnesota needed. — _TE_

**Update | 8:37 p.m.**Minnesota just got very lucky. Peterson fumbled at the New Orleans 45-yard line. Two Saints defenders had chances to recover, but the Vikings got it back at the expense of a 10-yard loss. — _TE_

**Update | 8:35 p.m.**Now we’ll see what the Vikings are made of. They took over at their own 20-yard line and are trailing for the first time. Their offense stalled for most of the second quarter. Favre needs to get back to dicing the Saints with short passes, as he did successfully in the first quarter. — _TE_

![Image 7: Despite the best efforts of Vikings safety Tyrell Johnson (25), Pierre Thomas found his way to the end zone to put the Saints ahead, 21-14.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/01/25/sports/25vikingsE/blogSpan.jpg)Chris Graythen/Getty Images Despite the best efforts of Vikings safety Tyrell Johnson (25), Pierre Thomas found his way to the end zone to put the Saints ahead, 21-14.

**Update | 8:30 p.m.**That was quick. The **Saints went ahead, 21-14**, with 12:56 left in third quarter on Thomas’s 9-yard touchdown run on the first possession of the second half. The drive covered 37 yards in four plays, and was set up Courtney Roby’s 61-yard kickoff return. — _TE_

**Update | 8:25 p.m.**Some interesting halftime stats:

— New Orleans ran only 25 plays versus 41 by the Vikings and converted only two of five third downs.

— Brees has thrown for more yards (133) than Favre (127), despite 10 fewer pass attempts.

— The Saints have struggled with penalties. They’ve been flagged five times for 45 yards; Minnesota has only two penalties for 10 yards. — _TE_

**Update | 8:13 p.m.**Just when the Vikings seemed poised to finish the second quarter ahead, they lost a fumble on a bad exchange between Favre and Peterson. Fujita recovered the ball at the 10-yard line, and Favre lay on the turf afterward with both hands on his helmet.

The Saints ran out the remaining 56 seconds of the first half. **Score: Vikings 14, Saints 14.** — _TE_

**Update | 8:11 p.m.**Those chants of “Reggie, Reggie, Reggie” just fell silent after Bush muffed a 39-yard punt that was recovered by the Vikings at the 10-yard line with 1:24 left. — _TE_

**Update | 8:09 p.m.**Another Saints punt, but the Vikings’ Bernard Berrian bobbled it and fell down before he was hit by a New Orleans defender, who was flagged for a personal foul, much to the displeasure of the crowd. Minnesota takes over at its own 32 with less than two minutes remaining in the second quarter. — _TE_

**Update | 8:04 p.m.**Favre’s passing has been fine today, but why don’t the Vikings give the ball to Peterson more? After all, he’s got 41 yards on just eight carries. Yes, nearly half of that total came on his 19-yard touchdown run in the first quarter, but it’s his threat to rip off a long run on every play that makes him so dangerous. — _TE_

**Update | 8:00 p.m.**Saints tight end Jeremy Shockey just caught a pass for 9 yards, a yard short of a first down. It was his first catch of the game. Shockey did not practice all week with a knee injury. After his catch, he seemed to limp a little. Shockey, who has not lined up for every play, is a potent weapon, when healthy. — _JL_

**Update | 7:57 p.m.**What once looked as if it would be a shootout has turned into a punting display. Minnesota just punted and Bush called for a fair catch at his team’s own 33-yard line. Every time Bush retreats to field a punt, the crowd chants, “Reggie, Reggie, Reggie.” It’s just waiting for him to make it erupt. — _TE_

**Update | 7:54 p.m.**New Orleans just blew a prime opportunity. On the heels of stopping the Vikings again, the Saints could only muster a disappointing three-and-out from deep in their own territory. Minnesota just took over at its own 24-yard line after a New Orleans punt. — _TE_

**Update | 7:51 p.m.**Minnesota advanced to its own 47-yard line before punting. That’s exactly what the Saints needed. Their defense finally seems to be settling down after stopping the Vikings on two straight possessions. — _TE_

**Update | 7:49 p.m.**Have to give it up to these rowdy Saints fans. One of them continues to beat on the turquoise press box, causing the first row of the press box to rattle. A few of my brethren in the news media look annoyed by this. Deal with it, folks. — _TE_

**Update | 7:45 p.m.**Despite [battling migraines](https://msn.foxsports.com/nfl/story/Minnesota-Vikings-Percy-Harvin-questionable-NFC-title-game-012210) this week, Harvin has looked unaffected so far. He’s been instrumental for the Vikings and already has team highs of four receptions for 33 yards to go along with two rushes for 10 yards. — _TE_

**Update | 7:41 p.m.**They’ve played 19 minutes 30 seconds, and we’ve seen 28 points.

The Saints tie it, 14-14, on a 9-yard touchdown pass from Brees to Devery Henderson. Early in the drive, Brees was missing the fingertips of his receivers by inches. Then he seemed to lock in his aim.

The scoring play might have been an ad-lib route by Henerson, after Brees bought time with a play-action handoff and a roll to the right. — _JL_

![Image 8: Devery Henderson, right, and David Thomas celebrate after Henderson pulled in a 9-yard touchdown pass from Drew Brees to even the score at 14-14.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/01/25/sports/25vikingsD/blogSpan.jpg)Justin Lane/European Pressphoto Agency Devery Henderson, right, and David Thomas celebrate after Henderson pulled in a 9-yard touchdown from Drew Brees to even the score at 14-14.

**Update | 7:37 p.m.**And the Saints come marching back. They just **tied the game at 14-14** on Brees’ beautiful 9-yard touchdown pass to the wide-open receiver Devery Henderson in the end zone with 10:30 left in the second quarter.

New Orleans seems to have the momentum for the first time this game. Stopping the Vikings on this drive would be a huge boost. — _TE_

**Update | 7:35 p.m.**This once-deafening crowd had lost some of its juice, but it just got re-energized by a 28-yard reception by Bush to the Minnesota 36-yard line. — _TE_

**Update | 7:31 p.m.**Finally, the Saints stop a Vikings drive. Favre made a good play just to throw an incompletion out of bounds under heavy pressure on third down. But he got hit again, hard, after delivering the pass. He has not yet been sacked, but has been knocked down at least four times, by my count.He is a 40-year-old athlete and it is clear the Saints, under defensive coordinator Gregg Williams, plan to wear him down. — _JL_

**Update | 7:28 p.m.**Still a lot of football to be played, but Minnesota looks unstoppable offensively so far. The Vikings have scored on both of their possessions while outgaining the Saints, 128-80. New Orleans better stop Minnesota on this drive or it could be in trouble. — _TE_

**Update | 7:25 p.m.**O.K., it’s early, it’s only the second quarter and Minnesota holds a 14-7 lead. But the Vikings seem to be playing with much more poise, even in the noise machine that is the Superdome.

Not only did the Saints hurt themselves with three penalties on defense during the last Vikings’ drive, but the Saints also looked desperate with that gadget play on the reverse to Reggie Bush, who did a pretty good job getting back to the line of scrimmage on what could have been a big loss. Bush had a great game last week against Arizona, with two touchdowns and 217 total yards. He has not been much of a factor yet today and is not known for putting together two consecutive good games. — _JL_

**Update | 7:23 p.m.**New Orleans can’t answer Minnesota on its second possession. It just went three-and-out and punted. The Vikings take over at their own 36-yard line. And that’s the end of the first quarter. **Minnesota 14, New Orleans 7**. — _TE_

**Update | 7:21 p.m.**New Orleans can’t figure out how to stop the Vikings. Favre just threw a 5-yard touchdown pass to wide receiver Sidney Rice to put Minnesota ahead, 14-7. The score was a dagger because it came on third down. The scoring drive covered 73 yards in 10 plays. — _TE_

![Image 9: After the Saints committed three defensive penalties in one drive, Brett Favre hit Sidney Rice in the end zone for a 5-yard touchdown pass and a 14-7 lead.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/01/25/sports/25vikingsC/blogSpan.jpg)Justin Lane/European Pressphoto Agency After the Saints committed three defensive penalties in one drive, Brett Favre hit Sidney Rice in the end zone for a 5-yard touchdown pass and a 14-7 lead.

**Update | 7:17 p.m.**On the Vikings’ second drive, the Saints really hurt themselves with three defensive penalties and paid for it when Favre hit Sidney Rice in the end zone for a 5-yard touchdown pass and a **14-7 lead** with 2:11 left in the first quarter.

The Saints managed to hit Favre hard again, after a handoff on an end-around to Percy Harvin. Then they hit him once more, the deed done this time by Darren Sharper on a safety blitz, even as Favre completed a pass for a 20-yard gain and a first down at the Saints’ 8.Favre seemed annoyed as he climbed to his feet. But the Saints’ defense spent most of the first quarter on the field. — _JL_

**Update | 7:12 p.m.**Minnesota picks up a first down to its own 37-yard line after Saints cornerback Randall Gay is flagged for holding Harvin after a Favre incompletion on third-and-5. The call appeared to be valid. — _TE_

**Update | 7:09 p.m.**After a 16-yard kickoff return by Harvin, the Vikings’ second possession starts at their own 27-yard line. Let’s see if the Saints have made any defensive adjustments after a brutal first series against Favre and Co. — _TE_

![Image 10: Pierre Thomas took a screen pass on the right side, weaved through six tacklers to tie the score at 7-7 in the first quarter.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/01/25/sports/25vikingsB/blogSpan.jpg)Jed Jacobsohn/Getty Images Pierre Thomas took a screen pass on the right side, weaved through six tacklers to tie the score at 7-7 in the first quarter.

**Update | 7:06 p.m.**This looks as if it could be a shootout. The Saints just tied the game at 7-7 on Brees’s 38-yard touchdown pass to Thomas. The reception was a career long for Thomas, who caught a screen pass behind the line of scrimmage and then went the distance. — _TE_

**Update | 7:04 p.m.**A screen pass works wonders against a great pass rush, and Brees just made the Vikings his victims as Pierre Thomas took a pass on the right side, weaved through six tacklers and crossed the goal line standing up on a 38-yard play to **tie the score at 7-7** with 6:30 left in the first quarter.These teams have powerful offenses.The fans are singing and dancing and chanting along to the “[Crunk](https://www.metrolyrics.com/halftime-stand-up-get-crunk-lyrics-ying-yang-twins.html)” song, and the press box is swaying to the rhythm. — _JL_

**Update | 7:00 p.m.**It’s early, but Brees is so far getting the pass protection he needs against the Vikings on New Orleans’s first possession. After starting at their own 24-yard line, the Saints just broke into Minnesota territory on an 8-yard run by Pierre Thomas to the Vikings’ 43. — _TE_

**Update | 6:57 p.m.**Well, this is exactly what the Saints feared. Peterson just reeled off a 19-yard touchdown run to stun this Superdome crowd and put the Vikings ahead, 7-0, with 9:35 left in the first quarter. It capped a 10-play, 80-yard drive that lasted 5:25. New Orleans had no answer for Favre, who diced the Saints by completing 6 of 7 passes for 47 yards. — _TE_

**Update | 6:54 p.m.**Adrian Peterson’s 19-yard touchdown run gave the Vikings a **7-0 lead** on the first drive of the game. Last week,against the Arizona Cardinals, the Saints also gave up a touchdown on the opening drive, except that drive took only one play and it was Tim Hightower going for 70 yards. Brett Favre was hit hard and knocked down on the first play from scrimmage, by linebacker Scott Fujita. His pass fell incomplete. After that, Favre completed six in a row. — _JL_

**Update | 6:49 p.m.**After an incompletion and getting hit on the game’s first play from scrimmage, Favre has settled in nicely. He’s now completed six straight passes for 47 yards and has the Vikings in field goal range. — _TE_

**Update | 6:45 p.m.**Minnesota wins the coin toss and elects to receive. We should get our first look at Harvin here. — _TE_

**Update | 6:40 p.m.**The Vikings were just greeted by a chorus of boos as they ran onto the field. One of the first to the sideline was tackle Zach Strief, who was particularly animated. He screamed and beat his chest. But the nearby Saints faithful were hardly intimidated. One fan appeared to greet Strief’s excitement by extending his middle finger. — _TE_

![Image 11: Adrian Peterson’s 19-yard touchdown run gave the Vikings a 7-0 lead on the first drive of the game.](https://static01.nyt.com/images/2010/01/25/sports/25vikingsA/blogSpan.jpg)Justin Lane/European Pressphoto Agency Adrian Peterson’s 19-yard touchdown run gave the Vikings a 7-0 lead on the first drive of the game.

**Preview:** Welcome to an energized Superdome, home of Who Dat Nation, for the N.F.C. Championship game between the visiting Vikings and the Saints.

It’s still 30 minutes to kickoff and fans are starting to trickle in from a wild, alcohol-infused scene outside on a sunny day with temperatures in the high 60s. Today’s winner will play the Indianapolis Colts, who defeated the Jets, 30-17, in the A.F.C. Championship Game.

With a win today, New Orleans would make their [first Super Bowl appearance](https://www.nytimes.com/2010/01/16/sports/football/16saints.html). It would continue a remarkable story of the Saints uniting this Hurricane Katrina-ravaged city and giving hope to its residents.

The Vikings are seeking a return to the Super Bowl for the first time since 1977. Appropriately, the former Vikings coach Bud Grant is Minnesota’s honorary captain today. He led the Vikings to four Super Bowls, including their last one in 1977.

The obvious story line is the play of Minnesota quarterback [Brett Favre](https://www.vikings.com/team/roster/Brett-Favre/1a6fce0d-f2d3-4314-bf36-645eddb20d6c) and New Orleans quarterback [Drew Brees](https://www.neworleanssaints.com/Team/Roster/People/Drew%20Brees.aspx), but just as important will be the Saints’ ability to keep the Vikings’ pass rush in check.

Minnesota leads the N.F.L. in sacks, so it’ll be important that Brees has time for the Saints’ high-powered offense to fire on all cylinders.

Vikings tailback [Adrian Peterson](https://www.vikings.com/team/roster/Adrian-Peterson/4dd7544a-5210-4aad-8e05-8ffb8cd92ddd) also figures to be a key, even though he hasn’t rushed for more than 100 yards since Week 10. But the Saints’ run defense is questionable and prone to giving up long runs, a specialty of Peterson’s.

But New Orleans has its own explosive threat in [Reggie Bush](https://www.neworleanssaints.com/Team/Roster/People/Reggie%20Bush.aspx), who had 217 all-purpose yards in [last week’s victory](https://www.nfl.com/gamecenter/2010011601/2009/POST19/cardinals@saints/watch) here against the Arizona Cardinals. It included a 46-yard touchdown run and an 83-yard punt return for a touchdown.

But also keep an eye on Minnesota’s dazzling wide receiver/kick returner Percy Harvin, the N.F.C. rookie of the year. He missed some practice time this week with migraine headaches, but is expected to play.

Expect a deafening crowd today. The chants of “Who Dat” have already started. — _TE_

**Pregame:** It is less than an hour before kickoff in the Superdome. Former President George H. W. Bush was just introduced. He is on the sideline, posing for pictures with players and dignitaries. He seems in no hurry to leave. Perhaps he will flip the coin with the teams’ captains before the game. His son, former President George W. Bush, was at the Dallas-Philadelphia game in the wild-card round. Gosh, that seems like a long time ago. — _JL_

**NEW ORLEANS** — The New Orleans Saints and the Minnesota Vikings play in domed stadiums that are loud but sterile. Besides the sound, neither facility provides much of a sense of place. But the franchises, geographically speaking, represent the northern headwaters of the Mississippi River (in Minnesota) and its southern basin (Louisiana and the Gulf of Mexico). It is the water spine of the map of North America, celebrated in song and literature.

Last night, in New Orleans, fog rolled in from the river, shrouding Jackson Square where the fortune tellers gather and the driver of a horse-drawn carriage took his passengers through weird little 19th-century streets. He told them tales of voodoo, slaves quarters, torture chambers, ghosts and vampires, and all the rest of that New Orleans mojo. Look, he said, halting the beast with his reins and pointing to his left. It’s the House of the Rising Sun, he said. And maybe it really was. — _JL_

==============================================================================

Garrett Hartley's kick sent Saints to their first Super Bowl
------------------------------------------------------------

 Jan 06, 2014 at 06:22 AM

NFC Championship Game In Review

K **Garrett Hartley** hit a 40-yard field goal straight through the uprights in overtime to give the Saints a 31-28 victory and the club's first trip to the Super Bowl. The Vikings took an early 7-0 lead on a 19-yard TD run by RB **Adrian Peterson**. The Saints tied the score when QB **Drew Brees** threw a screen to RB Pierre Thomas, which he took 38 yards for a TD. The Vikings took the lead back at the end of the first quarter on a five-yard scoring pass from QB **Brett Favre** to WR **Sidney Rice**. New Orleans took their first lead in the third quarter following a nine-yard TD pass from Brees to WR **Devery Henderson** and a nine-yard scoring run by Thomas. Peterson would run for two more TDs and CB **Tracy Porter** picked off Favre at the end of the fourth quarter to force overtime. The Saints opened up overtime with possession and scored on the drive.

Minnesota is 3-1 all-time against New Orleans in the playoffs and has advanced to or been in the NFC Championship in each of the past four postseasons in which the teams have met.

A mammoth blowout, a terrific tandem, a heartbreaking loss and a miraculous finish can describe the Vikings vantage point in the four previous playoff games with the Saints.

In honor of Throwback Thursday, here's a recap of those games:

### **Mammoth blowout**

Vikings 44, Saints 10

Jan. 3, 1988 | Superdome

**Setting the stage:** The 1987 season was shortened by one game because of a players' strike that resulted in the use of replacement players for three other games. Minnesota's fill-ins went 0-3 before starters returned to win five of six. They then lost three of four to close the season at 8-7 and eek into the playoffs (only five teams made it back then: three division winners and two Wild Card teams). A New Orleans team influenced by former Vikings General Manager Jim Finks closed with nine consecutive victories to earn the first trip to the postseason in franchise history. The Saints went 12-3 but finished second in the division as members of the NFC West behind San Francisco (13-2).

**In the game:** The Vikings started terribly, suffering a sack on their first play and a fumbled snap on their second play to give New Orleans the ball at the Minnesota 11. The Saints scored on their second offensive snap, but it was the only time they reached the end zone.

![Image 5: vikings-saints-history-1-2560](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/t_lazy/f_auto/vikings/btp8igklyefdaxjccwcd.jpg)

Al Messerschmidt/AP

An 84-yard punt return by Anthony Carter late in the first quarter gave the Vikings the lead for good.

Minnesota added a 5-yard touchdown pass from Wade Wilson (who relieved Tommy Kramer) to Steve Jordan, a 10-yard halfback pass from Allen Rice to Carter and a 44-yard Hail Mary pass from Wilson to Hassan Jones in the second quarter. The deep heave occurred on an untimed down after New Orleans was penalized for having 12 players on the field.

The Vikings defense limited the Saints to 11 completions and intercepted Bobby Hebert and Dave Wilson twice each to advance.

**Quote:** "I don't think anybody gave us a chance other than us. We went to New Orleans and kind of caught fire." — Ring of Honor LB Scott Studwell

### **Terrific tandem**

Vikings 34, Saints 16

Jan. 6, 2001 | Metrodome

![Image 6: vikings-saints-history-4-2560](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/t_lazy/f_auto/vikings/c3oknnybtv1ftb2t1lud.jpg)

Michael Conroy/AP

**Setting the stage:** The 2000 Vikings opened with seven consecutive wins and added a separate four-game win streak before dropping their final three games. Yet Minnesota won the NFC Central and a first-round bye with an 11-5 record. The Saints won the NFC West with a 10-6 mark that equaled the defending-champion Rams and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. New Orleans defeated St. Louis 31-28 in the Wild Card round.

**In the game:** A week after Isaac Bruce caught seven passes for 127 yards and a score and Torry Holt was limited to 26 yards on two catches, the Saints faced Minnesota's eventual Hall of Fame receivers Cris Carter and Randy Moss.

![Image 7: vikings-saints-history-3-2560](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/t_lazy/f_auto/vikings/nvzprc9kidqlxacuuwwf.jpg)

Michael Conroy/AP

Carter recorded eight catches for 120 yards and a score, nearly mirroring Bruce's line. Moss, like Holt, had two receptions, but they were for touchdowns of 53 and 68 yards from Daunte Culpepper.

Kailee Wong and Robert Tate each intercepted Aaron Brooks, who was sacked by John Randle and John Burrough.

**Quote:** "A lot of people have a lot of nicknames, but he has the nickname 'Super Freak' … When he plays at a high level, not many people in the league are better than him." — Cris Carter on Randy Moss

### **Heartbreaking loss**

Saints 31, Vikings 28

Jan. 24, 2010 | Superdome

![Image 8: vikings-saints-history-5-2560](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/t_lazy/f_auto/vikings/h8ymw8rtfftrvs4mbtcz.jpg)

Aaron M. Sprecher/AP

**Setting the stage:** The 2009 Vikings, led by former division rival Brett Favre, opened with six consecutive victories. The impressive start, however, was undermined when Minnesota went 2-3 in December, dropping three prime-time contests. The 12-4 mark was good enough for the No. 2 seed, and the Vikings routed the Cowboys in the Divisional round. The Saints opened even more impressively, winning their first 13 games, before losing their final three.

**In the game:** Vikings lead by seven, tie; Vikings lead 14-7, tie; Saints lead 21-14, tie; Saints lead 28-21, tie with 4:58 remaining.

Fred Evans recorded the Vikings lone sack of Drew Brees on the snap that followed a 2-yad touchdown run by Adrian Peterson.

Minnesota forced a three-and-punt and got the ball back at its own 21 with 2:37 remaining.

Completions by Favre of 10 and 20 yards were followed by a 14-yard run by Chester Taylor to the New Orleans 33 with 1:06 remaining. Runs by Taylor and Peterson were stuffed for no gain. Minnesota called a timeout with 19 seconds left on the clock.

![Image 9: vikings-saints-history-6-2560](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/t_lazy/f_auto/vikings/g39bs4zbvt1paesbgh7c.jpg)

Gerald Herbert/AP

The Vikings were then flagged for 12 men in the huddle, moving the ball to the 38. Favre, who had been pummeled throughout the game, tried to make a play with a late pass over the middle, and it was intercepted at the New Orleans 22 by Tracy Porter.

Minnesota never touched the ball again. Garrett Hartley made a 40-yard field goal to end the first overtime possession, which was helped by a phantom pass interference call.

**Quote:** "This season was a success. It's not the success we all wanted. But I have to tell you, this loss hurts – especially when we knew we should have won. It's hard to put the feeling I have right now into words. I felt we beat ourselves more than they beat us." — Bernard Berrian

### **Miraculous finish**

Vikings 29, Saints 24

Jan. 14, 2018 | U.S. Bank Stadium

![Image 10: vikings-saints-2-2560](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/t_lazy/f_auto/vikings/suhlfo5neuwevzfglmpl.jpg)

**Setting the stage:** The 2017 Vikings overcame a 2-2 start during which they lost their starting quarterback (Sam Bradford) and running back (Dalvin Cook) by winning 11 of 12 games to close the season. The 13-3 mark earned a No. 2 seed and the opportunity to host a Divisional round game. The Saints won a competitive NFC South with an 11-5 record, then hosted and defeated Carolina in the Wild Card round. New Orleans was again led by Brees and featured \_AP\_ Rookies of the Year on offense (Alvin Kamara) and defense (Marshon Lattimore).

**In the game:** The Vikings built a 17-0 lead by halftime with touchdown runs by Jerick McKinnon and Latavius Murray and kept the Saints off the scoreboard until 1:18 remained in the third quarter.

New Orleans surged with a pair of touchdown passes from Brees to Michael Thomas in a span of less than four minutes of game time. The Saints took a 21-20 lead on a 14-yard pass to Kamara with 3:01 remaining.

Minnesota responded with a 53-yard field goal by Kai Forbath with 1:29 to go. Brees converted a fourth-and-10 with a 13-yard pass for a first-and-10 at the Minnesota 33 with 40 seconds left.

Brian Robison and Anthony Harris stuffed Kamara for a loss of 1 on a third-and-1, and Minnesota used its second timeout with 29 seconds remaining.

Wil Lutz put the Saints up 24-23 on a 43-yard field goal.

Case Keenum converted a first-and-15 with a 19-yard pass to Diggs to move the ball to the Minnesota 39 with 18 seconds. A pair of incompletions followed, leaving Minnesota with 10 seconds and no timeouts.

![Image 11: vikings-saints-1-2560](https://static.clubs.nfl.com/image/private/t_editorial_landscape_mobile/t_lazy/f_auto/vikings/xk6c0ljamscykmzcgrx0.jpg)

Keenum aired out a pass that Stefon Diggs high-pointed. A subtle movement by Diggs helped him go unscathed on a tackle attempt by Marcus Williams. Diggs kept his balance, spun and cruised down the field for the winning score.

It was the first NFL playoff game to end with a touchdown as time expired and sent Vikings players, coaches and fans into unbelievable euphoria.

**Quote:** "I couldn't believe it. There are plays like this that you dream for your whole life." — Stefon Diggs

NFL conference championship game ratings (2002-present)
=======================================================

AFC and NFC Championship ratings dating back to the 2001-02 season. Dating back the 2002 playoffs, the most-watched NFL conference championship game was Vikings-Saints in 2010 (57.9M). That game and Giants-49ers in 2010 are tied as the highest rated (30.6).

On the other end of the spectrum, the lowest rated conference championship game was Panthers-Seahawks in 2006 (20.8) and the least-watched was Patriots-Steelers in 2002 (33.3M).

Nearly 60 million for Vikings/Saints thriller
=============================================

The Saints’ march to the Super Bowl attracted the largest non-Super Bowl TV audience in nearly 12 years.

Sunday’s Vikings/Saints NFC Championship Game drew a massive 30.6/45 fast-national rating and 57.9 million viewers on FOX, up 39% in ratings and 43% in viewers from Ravens/Steelers on CBS last year (22.0/34, 40.6 mil), and up 5% and 7%, respectively, from Giants/Packers on FOX in ’08 (29.0/43, 53.9 mil).

The game peaked with a 34.4/48 rating and 65.2 million viewers from 9:30-10 PM.

Vikings/Saints stands as the second-most viewed Conference Championship game in NFL history, behind only the 1982 Cowboys/49ers NFC title game on CBS (68.7 mil).

Additionally, the 30.6/45 rating is the highest for a Conference Championship game since Packers/Cowboys in ’96 (33.3/58).

To put the numbers in perspective, no World Series game has drawn a rating of 30.6 or higher since Braves/Twins Game 7 in ’91 (32.2/49), and no NBA Finals game has ever drawn a rating that high.

Vikings/Saints also drew a higher rating than every single primetime Olympics telecast — Summer or Winter — since ’94. That includes the ’96 Atlanta and ’02 Salt Lake City games.

Excluding the Super Bowl, the game ranks as the most-viewed television program on any network since the series finale of Seinfeld in ’98 (76.3 mil) — topping the previous 12-year high of 53.9 million for Giants/Packers in ’08 — and the most-viewed program in the history of the FOX network.

Overall, FOX averaged a 22.4/38 rating and 40.2 million viewers for its coverage of the NFL playoffs — the network’s highest rated postseason since ’97 and most-viewed ever.

===================================================

Favre throws interception in final seconds as Vikings fall
----------------------------------------------------------

BARRY WILNER The Associated Press

Jan. 24, 2010, 9:27 p.m. ET

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?display=popup&app_id=3847480411948529&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.blueridgenow.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2010%2F01%2F25%2Fsaints-in-their-first-super-bowl-after-overtime-win%2F28218200007%2F)[](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.blueridgenow.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2010%2F01%2F25%2Fsaints-in-their-first-super-bowl-after-overtime-win%2F28218200007%2F&text=Saints%20in%20their%20first%20Super%20Bowl%20after%20overtime%20win&via=BlueRidgeNow)[](mailto:?subject=Saints%20in%20their%20first%20Super%20Bowl%20after%20overtime%20win%20-%20from%20Hendersonville%20Times-News&body=Saints%20in%20their%20first%20Super%20Bowl%20after%20overtime%20win%0A%0ANEW%20ORLEANS%20%E2%80%94%20Unheralded%20Garrett%20Hartley%20lifted%20the%20New%20Orleans%20Saints%20into%20their%20first%20Super%20Bowl%20with%20a%2040-yard%20field%20goal%20in%20overtime%20for%20a%2031-28%20victory%20over%20the%20Minnesota%20Vikings%20for%20the%20NFC%20cha%E2%80%A6%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20blueridgenow.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.blueridgenow.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2F2010%2F01%2F25%2Fsaints-in-their-first-super-bowl-after-overtime-win%2F28218200007%2F)

Keep Watching

NEW ORLEANS — They sure ain't the Aints anymore.

The New Orleans Saints are heading to their first Super Bowl after battering Brett Favre and the Minnesota Vikings 31-28 in overtime Sunday on unheralded Garrett Hartley's 40-yard field goal.

The team that had no home five years ago after Hurricane Katrina ravaged its city and the Superdome overcame a slew of mistakes in the biggest game the Big Easy has ever seen.

But the biggest error was made by Favre. The 40-year-old quarterback threw away Minnesota's chance for its first Super Bowl trip in 33 years with an interception deep in Saints territory in the final seconds of regulation.

New Orleans won the coin toss, Drew Brees guided it to the Minnesota 22 and Hartley, suspended at the start of the season for using a banned stimulant, split the uprights 4:45 into OT.

"Just helping my team get to Miami," Hartley said. "Just doing my part."

Forget the paper bag masks and a long history of losing. Moments after Hartley's kick, they were toasting their hometown winners on Bourbon Street.

And in the Superdome, once a squalid refuge after Katrina, they boogied in the aisles as confetti covered the field.

The Saints (15-3) will meet the Peyton Manning and the Indianapolis Colts (16-2) in the Super Bowl in two weeks in Miami.

It's the first time the top seeds in each conference made the big game since the 1993 season.

N.F.L. Votes to Change Playoff Rules for Overtime
-------------------------------------------------

*   March 23, 2010

ORLANDO, Fla. — The N.F.L. approved a new [overtime rule](https://www.nytimes.com/2017/10/08/sports/nfl-overtime-rules.html) for the playoffs Tuesday that will give each team at least one possession in the extra period unless the team that wins the overtime coin toss scores a touchdown on its first possession.

After years of debate, the sentiment in favor of overtime reform was so strong — it passed by a surprisingly large margin, 28-4 — that it is possible owners will approve the rule for regular-season games in the 2010 season.

The only teams to vote against the rule change were Buffalo, Baltimore, Cincinnati and Minnesota, which [lost the N.F.C. championship game](http://www.nytimes.com/2010/01/25/sports/football/25nfc.html?scp=1&sq=vikings%20saints%20favre&st=cse "An article about the N.F.C. championship game.") last season after New Orleans won the overtime coin toss and kicked a winning field goal on its opening drive. That outcome could not happen with the new rule.

“We felt this year’s proposal gave us the opportunity to make a pretty good rule even better,” said Rich McKay, the Atlanta Falcons’ president and a member of the competition committee, which recommended the rule change. “I really believe the more you talk about the issue, the more you understand the statistics, the more you say there must be a change.”

The crux of the rule is to make overtime outcomes less dependent on the coin flip. If the team that has possession of the ball first scores a touchdown, the game is over. But if it kicks a field goal, the other team would get a possession and would win with a touchdown. If nobody scores on the first drives, or if both teams kick field goals, the game will revert to sudden death.

The change is expected to alter traditional overtime strategy. Bengals Coach Marvin Lewis said that the team with the first possession would have to consider going for a first down on fourth-and-short rather than attempting a lengthy field goal. And the team with the second possession — knowing what it needs to win, or at least to keep the game going — would be aware of when a field goal would be enough. That, McKay said, would offset the disadvantage of losing the coin toss.

Published: Jan 06, 2011 at 07:44 AM

NFL owners voted at the Annual Meeting in March to amend overtime rules for the postseason to a **MODIFIED SUDDEN DEATH** format. Teams will now have the opportunity to possess the ball at least once in the extra period unless the team that receives the overtime kickoff scores a touchdown on its first possession.

Here's a look at the NFL's overtime procedures for the postseason:

**POSTSEASON - MODIFIED SUDDEN DEATH**

The **modified sudden death**system of determining the winner shall prevail when the score is tied at the end of regulation playing time of postseason NFL games. The system guarantees each team a possession or the opportunity to possess, unless the team that receives the opening kickoff scores a touchdown on its initial possession.

» At the end of regulation time, the Referee will immediately toss a coin at the center of the field in accordance with rules pertaining to the usual pregame toss. The captain of the visiting team will call the toss prior to the coin being flipped.

» Following a three-minute intermission after the end of the regulation game, play will be continued in 15-minute periods until a winner is declared. Each team must possess or have the opportunity to possess the ball unless the team that has the ball first scores a touchdown on its initial possession. Play continues in sudden death until a winner is determined, and the game automatically ends upon any score (by safety, field goal, or touchdown) or when a score is awarded by the Referee for a palpably unfair act. Each team has three time-outs per half and all general timing provisions apply as during a regular game. The try is not attempted if a touchdown is scored. Disqualified players are not allowed to return.

» Instant Replay: No challenges. Reviews to be initiated by the replay assistant.

**» Possession:** Actual possession of the ball with complete control. The defense gains possession when it catches, intercepts, or recovers a loose ball.

**» Opportunity to possess:** The opportunity to possess occurs only during kicking plays. A kickoff is an opportunity to possess for the receiving team. If the kicking team legally recovers the kick, the receiving team is considered to have had its opportunity. A punt or a field goal that crosses the line of scrimmage and is muffed by the receiving team is considered to be an opportunity to possess for the receivers. Normal touching rules by the kicking team apply.

There have been 27 overtime postseason games, starting with the 1958 NFL Championship.

**POSTSEASON OVERTIME HISTORY - CHRONOLOGICAL**

The playoffs have featured at least one overtime game in nine of the past 10 postseasons, including two last year.

A look at NFL overtime playoff games since 2000:

An overtime history of the 2010 playoff participants:

Following are the Approved Rulings pertaining to postseason overtime as found on pages 106-108 of the 2010 Official Casebook of the NFL:

**A.R. 16.1 KICKOFF RETURN FOR TOUCHDOWN**  
Team B receives the opening kickoff and returns it for a touchdown.  
**Ruling:** Game over. Team B wins.

**A.R. 16.2 ONSIDE KICK**  
On the opening kickoff of overtime, Team A legally recovers the ball at the A41.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on A41. A kickoff is considered an opportunity to possess for the receiving team. Team B is considered to have had an opportunity to possess the ball.

**A.R. 16.3 ONSIDE KICK**  
On the opening kickoff of overtime, Team A attempts an onside kick. A2 legally touches the ball at the A42 but muffs it and it is recovered by B1 at the A43.  
**Ruling:** B's ball, first-and-10 on A43. Team A is not considered to have had an opportunity to possess the ball.

**A.R. 16.4 MUFFED KICKOFF**  
Following a successful field goal on the opening possession of overtime, Team A's kickoff is muffed by B1 at the B35 and is recovered by A2.  
**Ruling:** Game over. Team A wins. Team B had an opportunity to possess the ball.

**A.R. 16.5 TOUCHDOWN ON FIRST POSSESSION**  
Team A drives down the field on the opening possession of overtime and scores a touchdown.  
**Ruling:** Game over. Team A wins.

**A.R. 16.6 FIELD GOAL ON FIRST POSSESSION**  
Team A kicks a field goal on the opening possession of overtime.  
**Ruling:** Three points for Team A, but the game is not over. Team A must kick off to Team B. If Team B scores a touchdown or does not score the game is over. If Team B scores a field goal the game continues under sudden death.

**A.R. 16.7 MUFFED PUNT**  
On the opening possession of overtime, Team A punts and B3 muffs the punt at the B20. A6 recovers at the B22.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on B22. Team B had the opportunity to possess the kick. Both teams have met the minimum requirements for possession and the first team to score wins.

**A.R. 16.8 FUMBLED KICKOFF RETURN**  
On the opening kickoff of overtime, B3 returns the ball to the B30 where he is hit and fumbles. A6 muffs the loose ball to the B28 where B5 recovers.  
**Ruling:** B's ball, first-and-10 on B28. Since the ball was loose from a fumble as opposed to a kick, Team A is not considered to have had an opportunity to possess the ball.

**A.R. 16.9 BLOCKED PUNT**  
Fourth-and-5 on A45. On the opening possession of overtime, Team A's punt is blocked by B3 at the A35. A2 picks up the loose ball at the A40 and runs to the 50 for a first down.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on 50. Team B is not considered to have had an opportunity to possess the ball because it did not touch the ball beyond the line of scrimmage.

**A.R. 16.10 BLOCKED PUNT**  
Fourth-and-5 on A45. On the opening possession of overtime, Team A's punt is blocked by B3 at the A35. B4 attempts to pick up the loose ball at the A40 but muffs it to the A33 where it is recovered by A4 who runs to the B40 for a first down.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on B40. Team B is not considered to have had an opportunity to possess the ball because it did not touch the ball beyond the line of scrimmage.

**A.R. 16.11 BLOCKED PUNT**  
Fourth-and-5 on A45. On the opening possession of overtime, Team A's punt is blocked by B3 at the A35. The ball hits the ground beyond the line at the B48 and bounces back to the A43 where it is recovered by A4 who runs to the B40 for a first down.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on B40. Team B is not considered to have had an opportunity to possess the ball because it did not touch the ball beyond the line of scrimmage.

**A.R. 16.12 BLOCKED PUNT**  
Fourth-and-5 on A45. On the opening possession of overtime, Team A's punt is blocked by B3 at the A35. The ball bounces beyond the line to the A48, where B4 muffs the loose ball to the A45 where it is recovered by A4.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on A45. By touching the punt beyond the line of scrimmage, a new series is awarded to Team A. Since Team B had the opportunity to possess the ball, both teams have met the minimum requirements for possession.

**A.R. 16.13 FUMBLE**  
Third-and-5 on A30. On the opening possession of overtime, A2 takes a handoff and runs to the B35 where he fumbles the ball. B2 recovers the ball and runs to the B40.  
**Ruling:** B's ball, first-and-10 on B40. Both teams have had an actual possession and the first team to score wins.

**A.R. 16.14 FUMBLE**  
Third-and-5 on A30. On the opening possession of overtime, A2 takes a handoff and runs to the B35 where he fumbles the ball. B2 recovers the ball and runs to the B40 where he is hit and fumbles. A5 recovers at the B41.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on B41. Both teams have possessed the ball and the first team to score wins.

**A.R. 16.15 INTERCEPTION**  
Third-and-5 on A30. On the opening possession of overtime, B2 intercepts a pass at the 50 and returns it for a touchdown.  
**Ruling:** Game over. Team B wins. Each team has had an actual possession.

**A.R. 16.16 FUMBLE**  
Second-and-10 on A30. On the opening possession of overtime, A2 takes a handoff and runs to the A38 where he fumbles the ball. B2 muffs the loose ball at the A35 and it is recovered by A5 at the A33.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, third-and-7 on A33. Since the ball was loose from a fumble as opposed to a kick, Team B is not considered to have had an opportunity to possess the ball.

**A.R. 16.17 TOUCHING OF A PASS**  
Third-and-5 on A30. On the opening possession of overtime, A1 drops back to pass and throws the ball from the A23. The ball is tipped by defensive lineman B4 at the A25 and is caught by tight end A3 at the A34. A3 runs to the A40 where he is tackled.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on A40. Touching of a pass by Team B does not constitute an opportunity to possess the ball.

**A.R. 16.18 INCOMPLETE PASS**  
Second-and-5 on A30. On the opening possession of overtime, A1 drops back to pass and throws the ball from the A23 toward receiver A2 at the B40. Cornerback B4 jumps up to intercept the pass and lands with his left foot inbounds and his right foot on the sideline.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, third-and-5 on A30. An incomplete pass is not considered an opportunity to possess.

**A.R. 16.19 SAFETY**  
Third-and-5 on A7. On the opening possession of overtime, A1 is tackled in his own end zone for a safety.  
**Ruling:** Game over. Team B wins. Both teams have met the minimum requirements for possession.

**A.R. 16.20 FIELD GOAL**  
Fourth-and-5 on B25. On the opening possession of overtime, Team A's field-goal attempt is blocked by B3 at the line of scrimmage and lands at the B28 where it is recovered by A4 who runs to the B18 for a first down.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on B18. Team B is not considered to have had an opportunity to possess the ball because it did not touch the ball beyond the line of scrimmage.

**A.R. 16.21 FIELD GOAL**  
Fourth-and-5 on B25. On the opening possession of overtime, Team A's field-goal attempt is blocked by B3 at the line of scrimmage. The ball hits the ground beyond the line at the B22 and bounces back to the B28 where it is recovered by A4 who runs to the B18 for a first down.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on B18. Team B is not considered to have had an opportunity to possess the ball because it did not touch the ball beyond the line of scrimmage.

**A.R. 16.22 FIELD GOAL**  
Fourth-and-5 on B25. On the opening possession of overtime, Team A's field-goal attempt is blocked by B3 at the line of scrimmage. The ball bounces beyond the line to the B20, where B4 muffs the loose ball to the B18 where it is recovered by A4.  
**Ruling:** A's ball, first-and-10 on B18. Because Team B touched the kick beyond the line of scrimmage, a new series is awarded to Team A. Since Team B had the opportunity to possess the ball, both teams have met the minimum requirements for possession.

FOX SPORTS CAPS OFF RECORD-SETTING NFL SEASON WITH MOST-WATCHED CONFERENCE CHAMPIONSHIP GAME IN ALMOST 30 YEARS

58 Million Viewers Tune In To See Unforgettable Vikings/Saints Epic Overtime Thriller;

Second Only To Cowboys/49ers "The Catch" Classic in 1982

Contest Posts +40% Gain Over Last Year's Eagles/Cardinals NFC Title Tilt

New Orleans Delivers Highest Local Rating for a Postseason NFL Game Ever

Yesterday's epic 2010 NFC CHAMPIONSHIP GAME on FOX between the New Orleans Saints and Minnesota Vikings delivered an extraordinary 30.6/45 household rating/share and averaged over 57.9 million viewers, according to fast national figures released by Nielsen Media Research. The overtime battle not only produced the biggest audience ever for an NFC Championship Game on FOX, it is also the second largest audience for any conference championship game, trailing only the 1982 Cowboys-49ers (Montana-to-Clark "The Catch") NFC Championship Game (68.7 million viewers on CBS). Excluding Super Bowl broadcasts, last night's average audience of 57.9 million ascends the 2010 NFC CHAMPIONSHIP GAME to television's most-watched program since the 1998 "Seinfeld" series finale (76.3 million viewers). It also ranks as the eighth most-watched show in the history of FOX, trailing only the network's five Super Bowls and two Super Bowl postgame shows.

Last night's fast national rating of 30.6/45 is a +40% gain over last year's 21.9/41 for Eagles-Cardinals in the early window and the highest rating for a conference championship game in 14 years (33.3/58 � Packers/Cowboys in 1996.) Ratings climbed to Super Bowl-like levels as the game progressed toward overtime, peaking at an astounding 34.4/48 rating and 65.2 million viewers from 9:30 � 10:00 PM ET.

New Orleans delivered a 63.2/82 last night, the highest local rating for a postseason NFL game ever, beating the home market rating of every team that has ever played in a Super Bowl. Viewing in New Orleans peaked at a 67.4/86 at 10:15 PM as Garrett Hartley drilled a 40-yard field goal to send the Saints to their first-ever Super Bowl.

Minneapolis posted a 58.7/80 last night, which is in its own right the third highest local rating ever for an NFC playoff game on FOX, trailing only New Orleans for yesterday's game and Milwaukee in the 1997 Championship Game. Milwaukee was yesterday's No. 3 market at a 47.4/64 as Packer fans tuned-in in droves to watch Brett Favre's championship bid.

The 2010 NFC PLAYOFFS go down in the record books as FOX's most-watched ever. FOX's four NFC Playoff games averaged 40.2 million viewers, besting the previous mark of 37.3 million set in 1995. Not only is this FOX's largest NFC Playoff viewership ever, it is the best for the NFC Playoffs on either FOX or CBS since Nielsen introduced the people meter during the 1987-88 season. This year's four NFC Playoff games averaged a 22.4/38 household rating/share, a +24% gain over last year's 18.1/33 and FOX's best since 1997 (23.7/48).

NFL on FOX makes playoff ratings history
========================================

By [FoxSports](https://www.foxsports.com/)

Published January 26, 2010 10:54pm EST | Updated [January 8, 2015 3:13pm EST](https://www.foxnews.com/html-sitemap/2015/january/8)

Sunday's epic 2010 NFC Championship on FOX between the [New Orleans Saints](http://www.foxnews.com/topics/football/new-orleans-saints.htm#r_src=ramp) and [Minnesota Vikings](http://www.foxnews.com/topics/football/minnesota-vikings.htm#r_src=ramp) delivered an extraordinary 30.6/45 household rating/share and averaged over 57.9 million viewers, according to fast national figures released by Nielsen Media Research.

The overtime battle not only produced the biggest audience ever for an NFC Championship Game on FOX, it is also the second largest audience for any conference championship game, trailing only the 1982 Cowboys-49ers (Montana-to-Clark "The Catch") NFC Championship Game (68.7 million viewers on CBS).

Excluding [Super Bowl](http://www.foxnews.com/topics/football/super-bowl.htm#r_src=ramp) broadcasts, last night's average audience of 57.9 million ascends the 2010 NFC Championship to television's most-watched program since the 1998 "Seinfeld" series finale (76.3 million viewers). It also ranks as the eighth most-watched show in the history of FOX, trailing only the network's five Super Bowls and two Super Bowl postgame shows.

![Image 31: placeholder](https://static.foxnews.com/static/v/all/img/clear.gif)

Sunday night's fast national rating of 30.6/45 is a +40% gain over last year's 21.9/41 for Eagles-Cardinals in the early window and the highest rating for a conference championship game in 14 years (33.3/58 – Packers/Cowboys in 1996.) Ratings climbed to Super Bowl-like levels as the game progressed toward overtime, peaking at an astounding 34.4/48 rating and 65.2 million viewers from 9:30-10 p.m. ET.

New Orleans delivered a 63.2/82 last night, the highest local rating for a postseason NFL game ever, beating the home market rating of every team that has ever played in a Super Bowl. Viewing in New Orleans peaked at a 67.4/86 at 10:15 p.m. as [Garrett Hartley](http://www.foxnews.com/topics/football/new-orleans-saints/garrett-hartley.htm#r_src=ramp) drilled a 40-yard field goal to send the Saints to their first-ever Super Bowl.

Minneapolis posted a 58.7/80 last night, which is in its own right the third highest local rating ever for an NFC playoff game on FOX, trailing only New Orleans for yesterday's game and Milwaukee in the 1997 Championship Game. Milwaukee was yesterday's No. 3 market at a 47.4/64 as Packer fans tuned-in in droves to watch Brett Favre's championship bid.

The 2010 NFC Playoffs go down in the record books as FOX's most-watched ever. FOX's four NFC Playoff games averaged 40.2 million viewers, besting the previous mark of 37.3 million set in 1995. Not only is this FOX's largest NFC Playoff viewership ever, it is the best for the NFC Playoffs on either FOX or CBS since Nielsen introduced the people meter during the 1987-88 season. This year's four NFC Playoff games averaged a 22.4/38 household rating/share, a +24% gain over last year's 18.1/33 and FOX's best since 1997 (23.7/48).

15.title: T3duZXJzIGFwcHJvdmUgbmV3IHBsYXllci1zYWZldHkgcnVsZXMsIHdlaWdoIGV4cGFuZGluZyBPVCBydWxl
15.content:
Published: Mar 24, 2010 at 07:18 AM

ORLANDO, Fla. -- Players should be safer during games because of several rules changes approved at the NFL Annual Meeting. They also might be playing longer in regular-season overtimes.

The NFL passed rules Wednesday to further protect defenseless players, including ball carriers who lose their helmet during a play. Seven of eight overall rules proposals were adopted, then several owners said they also expect the [modified playoff overtime](https://www.nfl.com/news/story?id=09000d5d8171b356&template=with-video-with-comments&confirm=true) that passed the previous day to be revisited in May to include the regular season.

"It's a better system, so why not have a better system every game?" [Philadelphia Eagles](https://www.nfl.com/teams/philadelphiaeagles/profile?team=PHI) owner Jeffrey Lurie said of expanding the new OT rule that allows a team losing the coin toss and allowing a field goal on the first series to then have a possession.

[New York Giants](https://www.nfl.com/teams/newyorkgiants/profile?team=NYG) owner John Mara added he expects discussion and possibly a vote on using the new OT system to occur at the owners meetings in Dallas in May. The change was proposed only for the postseason by the competition committee and was passed 28-4 Tuesday.

NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell said the league wants to meet with the players and television networks for some input and further discuss the ramifications of expanding the OT change.

"We had a proposal for the postseason, we passed that with the understanding that it'll be discussed for the regular season," he said.

Goodell also mentioned scheduling only intradivision games on the final weekend of the season, and [placing many such games in Week 16](http://www.nfl.com/news/story?id=09000d5d8171ff2f&template=with-video-with-comments&confirm=true), as well. He said at the end of last season that he was concerned about teams not playing their regulars after clinching titles and is hopeful different scheduling would help avoid that issue.

The 2010 schedule will be released in April.

The key rules change for player safety bars a defenseless player from being hit in the head or neck area by an opponent who launches himself and uses his helmet, shoulder or forearm to make contact. Previously, those kind of tackles were banned against receivers who couldn't protect themselves, but now it will apply to everyone.

"These are very specific to very vulnerable moments in the game," Lurie said. "There's no reason not to protect these players. There's a history of potentially serious injuries in these types of collisions."

NFL rules also will echo those in college when a player running with the ball loses his helmet. The whistle will blow immediately and the ball will be placed at the "progress spot" where the helmet came off.

The umpire now will be stationed behind the offensive backfield rather than in the linebackers area after the competition committee saw "a hundred" examples of umpires being run over.

»  During a field-goal or extra-point attempt, the defensive team can't position any player on the line directly across from the snapper. Previously, a player needed to have his helmet outside the snapper's shoulder pads.

»  A dead-ball personal foul on the final play of the second or fourth quarters will cause a 15-yard penalty on the second half or overtime kickoff. Previously in those situations, no penalty was enforced, although players subsequently could be fined by Goodell.

»  If a punt returner makes a fair-catch signal and muffs the ball, he is entitled to "reasonable opportunity" to recover before it hits the ground without interference of the coverage team. The ball will be rewarded at the spot of the interference, but there will be no penalty yardage marked off.

»  When a ball strikes a videoboard (as one punt did last preseason at the new [Cowboys](https://www.nfl.com/teams/dallascowboys/profile?team=DAL) Stadium), guide wire or sky cam, the play is whistled dead and replayed. The game clock is reset to when that play started.

The replay judge will be allowed to initiate a review if he believes there was some sort of interference with the ball. This is the only case outside of the final two minutes of the second and fourth quarters and overtime that the booth can order a replay.

Coaches also can challenge whether there was interference with the ball.

»  If the clock is stopped in the final minute of either half for a replay review but wouldn't have stopped without the review, officials will run off 10 seconds before resuming play. Either team could take a timeout to void the 10-second runoff.
